newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to issue fire equipment rule for cargo holds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to issue fire equipment rule for cargo holds.

text.p: All cargo holds in U.S. passenger jets would be required to have fire detection and suppression equipment under a proposed rule the Federal Aviation Admninistration expects to issue later Tuesday.
The rule comes over a year after ValuJet flight 592 plunged into the Florida Everglades, killing all 110 people aboard, after a fire occurred in the cargo hold.
Airlines are expected to be given up to three years to fit the equipment once a final rule is issued. An FAA spokeswoman said the agency was looking to produce that final rule by the end of the year.

The equipment, consisting of smoke detectors and a halon gas fire suppression system, would be fitted to Class D cargo holds in over 3,000 U.S. aircraft that currently rely on an air-tight seal and a fire-resistant liner as their defence against fires.
It is unlikely that halon gas could have extinguished or significantly slowed the fire on the ValuJet flight.
But industry safety experts say the fire detectors might have warned the crew earlier and led to an aborted takeoff or an earlier attempt to return to Miami airport.
Airlines agreed to fit the new fire equipment at a meeting last December at the White House.
The National Transportation Safety Board and lawmakers have criticised the FAA and the industry for not moving more aggressively to implement the new rules.
An industry source said last week that the airlines were still willing to start installing the fire equipment before FAA's final rule was issued.
But there had been delays in waiting for the Environmental Protection Agency to issue a waiver for using halon gas and for the FAA to agree to the outline of the rule.

The source, who requested anonymity, said the airlines were working with Boeing to speed up the delivery date of kits for Boeing 727 and 737 aircraft to December of this year from the third quarter of 1998.
Other aircraft types affected by the rule include McDonnell Douglas, Fokker, Lockheed 11011s and Airbus A320s.
The airline industry estimates the cost of the changes will be around $50,000 to $70,000 per aircraft.
